case.title: Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017), Section 3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention
case.excerpt: 3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention. The attention used is called "Scaled Dot-Product Attention". The input consists of queries and keys of dimension d_k, and values of dimension d_v. The dot products of the query with all keys are computed, each is divided by sqrt(d_k), and a softmax function is applied to obtain the weights on the values. In practice the attention function is computed on a set of queries simultaneously, packed together into a matrix Q; the keys and values are packed into matrices K and V. The matrix of outputs is computed as: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V   (Equation 1). The two most commonly used attention functions are additive attention and dot-product (multiplicative) attention. Dot-product attention is identical to this algorithm except for the scaling factor 1/sqrt(d_k). Additive attention computes the compatibility function using a feed-forward network with a single hidden layer. The two are similar in theoretical complexity, but dot-product attention is faster and more space-efficient in practice because it can use optimized matrix multiplication. For small d_k the two mechanisms perform similarly, but additive attention outperforms dot-product attention without scaling for larger d_k. The authors suspect that for large d_k the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax into regions where it has extremely small gradients; to counteract this, the dot products are scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k). Footnote 4: to illustrate why the dot products get large, assume the components of q and k are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1; then their dot product q . k = sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i has mean 0 and variance d_k.
case.focus: Explain scaled dot-product attention (Section 3.2.1, Equation 1) using small, editable Q, K, and V matrices. Show similarity scores, normalized attention weights, and the output. Let the learner edit values and switch scaling on/off. Guide them through equal scores and a dominant score. Check that each row of weights sums to one and that the output equals the weighted sum of V. Do not train a Transformer.
case.audience: Engineering undergraduate who knows matrix multiplication and dot products but has not studied Transformers.

plan.concept: Scaled dot-product attention: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V, computed on small editable Q, K, V matrices.
plan.computation: Given Q (n_q x d_k), K (n_k x d_k), V (n_k x d_v): compute raw scores S = Q K^T (n_q x n_k), scale by 1/sqrt(d_k) (toggleable), softmax each row to get weights A (n_q x n_k), then output O = A V (n_q x d_v). Also report row sums of A, and the weighted-sum interpretation of each output row.
plan.visual: Left: heatmap of scores S (or scaled scores) with row/col labels. Middle: heatmap of attention weights A with row sums annotated. Right: bars of output rows O. Arrows show the cause->effect chain Q,K -> scores -> weights -> output.
plan.controls: n_q, n_k, d_k, d_v as number controls (1..4); Q, K, V as editable matrices sized by those controls; a toggle for scaling on/off.
plan.checks: Each row of A sums to 1; O equals the weighted sum of V rows using A; scaling toggle changes scores by factor 1/sqrt(d_k); equal keys give equal weights; dominant score gives weight near 1.

spec.title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention (Equation 1)
spec.hook: Edit small Q, K and V matrices and watch how dot products become attention weights and then a weighted average of the values.
spec.idea:
Attention lets each query look at all keys, decide how similar they are, and then take a weighted average of the values. The similarity is just a dot product: $q \cdot k$. Because dot products can grow with dimension, the paper divides them by $\sqrt{d_k}$ before the softmax.

The softmax turns a row of scores into a probability distribution: all weights are positive and sum to one. The output for that query is then the weighted sum of the value rows.

In matrix form, all queries are processed at once: $\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}(Q K^T / \sqrt{d_k}) V$. Here $Q$ is $n_q \times d_k$, $K$ is $n_k \times d_k$, and $V$ is $n_k \times d_v$.

This page is a toy calculator: no training, no datasets, just the forward computation on numbers you choose.
spec.why: Scaled dot-product attention is the core operation inside every Transformer. Understanding the shapes, the scaling factor and the softmax row-sum property makes the rest of the architecture much easier to read.

equations.tex: S = Q K^T, \quad S_{ij} = q_i \cdot k_j
equations.caption: Raw similarity scores between query $i$ and key $j$.
Attention weights: each row is a probability distribution.

equations.tex: O = A V, \quad o_i = \sum_j A_{ij} v_j
equations.caption: Output: each row is a weighted sum of the value rows.

spec.visual_caption: Left heatmap: raw scores $S = QK^T$ (or scaled scores when the toggle is on). Middle heatmap: attention weights $A$; each row sums to 1. Right bars: output rows $O = AV$. Arrows show the computation order.

explorations.title: Equal scores
explorations.change: Look at the middle heatmap, then change one entry of K.
explorations.observe: With all keys equal, every weight in the row is $1/3$ and the output is the average of the value rows. Changing one key entry breaks the tie.
explorations.why: Equal scores give equal softmax inputs, so the softmax output is uniform.

explorations.title: Dominant score
explorations.change: Increase the first entry of Q toward 3 and watch the first weight.
explorations.observe: The first weight approaches 1 and the output approaches the first value row. Turning scaling off makes this even sharper.
explorations.why: A large score dominates the softmax, so its weight approaches 1.

pitfall.title: Softmax is not a similarity score
pitfall.text: The raw dot products $S$ are similarities, but the attention weights $A$ are normalized probabilities. Only $A$ rows sum to one; $S$ rows do not.
